To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Drosophila melanogastrer flies can distinguish between the two chemically very similar sugars D-arabinose and L-arabinose.
Drosophila flies prefer D-arabinose over L-arabinose, but they form long-term memories of the latter more reliably.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how the brain represents the value of a reward and how it translates this value into behavior.
the neural mechanisms underlying the ability of animals to form long-term memories of rewards and to use these memories to guide future behavior.
the question of how animals perceive and learn to value rewards, such as sugars, that they encounter.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Drosophila can discriminate between D- and L-arabinose, and that this discrimination is mediated by the sugar receptor Gr43A.
Drosophila melanogastric preferentially D-arabinose to L-arabinose, but form long-term memory for L-arabinose.
D-arabinose is a more rewarding sugar for flies than L-arabinose, as flies prefer it over L-arabinose and learn to avoid L-arabinose better.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that Drosophila melanostater can perceive the difference between L- and D- arabinose sugars.
Drosophila flies prefer D- arabinose over L- arabi- nose in a short term behavioral assay, while they learn about the value of L- arabin- ose more reliably than D-arabinose.
Drosophila can distinguish two similar sugars, L-arabinose and D-arabinoses based on their immediate valence and the long-term memory they generate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immediate perception of a reward and the reward’s long term salience can be distinct.
the immediate perception of a reward may not be predictive of the long term salience of that same reward, and that distinct sensory neurons may generate distinct reward representations.
immediate reward valence is distinct from long-term reward salience, and that the two are not always correlated.
